1.title: Basic Labelling Principles
1.html:
• Like all Alsace wines, bottling in the region of origin is mandatory — even for the top Grand Cru
  • For the base Alsace AOC tier, whether the label shows a variety name is optional (not mandatory)
  • Apart from the two blending exceptions (Altenberg de Bergheim, Kaefferkopf), Grand Cru labels normally show the variety name
  • Grand Cru labels must show both the vintage and the site name (lieu-dit) — both are required
2.title: "Pinot" and "Klevner": One Label, Four Possibilities
2.html:
This is one of the most surprising details in Alsace labelling rules: when the label says "Pinot" or "Klevner", it may be any of the following, or a blend of them:

Auxerrois B
Pinot Blanc B
Pinot Noir N (vinified as white)
Pinot Gris G

In other words, when you see "Alsace Pinot" on a label, the label alone does not tell you which Pinot-family variety (or varieties) it is made from — which is why many quality estates add a more precise variety name such as "Pinot Blanc" on the label.
3.title: Edelzwicker vs Gentil: Two Blending Philosophies
3.items.0.desc: Any blend of Alsace white grape varieties, with no fixed proportions and no obligation to disclose them; varieties may be vinified separately or together. The label does not (and may not) list variety names. The representative everyday table wine: fresh, easy to drink, not made for ageing.
3.items.1.desc: A "quality blend" governed by the interprofessional charter (Charte Interprofessionnelle): at least 50% must come from Riesling, Muscat, Pinot Gris and Gewurztraminer (the noble varieties), with the rest made up by Sylvaner, Chasselas and Pinot Blanc. Each variety must first be certified AOC Alsace on its own before blending, and the bottled wine must pass a tasting certification before release.
4.question: What does "Alsace Pinot" on an Alsace label mean?
4.options.0: Always a red wine made from 100% Pinot Noir
4.options.1: It may be one of Auxerrois, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir (vinified as white) or Pinot Gris, or a blend of them — the exact variety cannot be known from the label alone
4.options.2: Always a half-and-half blend of Pinot Blanc and Pinot Gris
4.options.3: It is an illegal way of labelling
4.explanation: Alsace regulations allow "Pinot" or "Klevner" as a collective designation for any one of the four varieties Auxerrois B, Pinot Blanc B, Pinot Noir N (vinified as white) and Pinot Gris G, or a blend of them. This is one of the details of Alsace labelling most likely to mislead consumers — seeing "Pinot" does not mean it is Pinot Blanc.
5.keyPoints.0: All Alsace wines (including Grand Cru) must be bottled in the region of origin — mandatory
5.keyPoints.1: "Pinot" / "Klevner" can mean Auxerrois, Pinot Blanc, Pinot Noir (vinified white) or Pinot Gris, or a blend of them
5.keyPoints.2: Apart from the two blending exceptions, Grand Cru usually shows the variety name, and must show both vintage and site name
5.keyPoints.3: Edelzwicker: free blend, no variety shown; Gentil: governed by the interprofessional charter, ≥50% noble varieties, vinified separately and blended after certification
